questions.text: What is a branch circuit under the checked PEC definition?

options.text: The conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets.
The utility-owned transformer only.
The room finish schedule.
The water service pipe.

questions.rationale: PEC defines a branch circuit by its endpoints: final overcurrent device to outlets.

questions.text: What is a feeder under the checked PEC definition?

options.text: The circuit conductors between service equipment or another source and the final branch-circuit overcurrent device.
Only a luminaire whip after the final breaker.
Only a wall switch leg.
A plumbing waste line.

questions.rationale: PEC defines a feeder by its location upstream of final branch-circuit overcurrent protection.
questions.explanation: 300 kVA is below calculated 282.35 kVA; marginal selection that ignores future growth. 350 kVA is not a standard transformer rating; must select from standard sizes. 400 kVA is not a standard rating in the Philippine transformer market. Calculation: Demand Load = 300 kW × 0.80 = 240 kW. kVA = 240 ÷ 0.85 = 282.35 kVA. The next standard transformer size per PEC Part 4 (Transformers) is 300 kVA, but 300 kVA is below the calculated 282.35 kVA; to provide a safety margin and accommodate future growth, the next available standard rating above 282.35 kVA is 500 kVA (since 300 kVA is only marginally above and may be insufficient for inrush and future expansion). Transformer sizing must account for both demand factors and power factor, then select from standard sizes (PEC Part 4). Always round up to accommodate growth and inrush current.

Outlets, branch circuits, utility service, feeder, panelboard.

questions.explanation: Power factor correction uses tan θ calculations, not √3 in the basic voltage drop formula. Reactive power (kVAR) is calculated separately; √3 is purely a geometric voltage relationship. 60 Hz frequency is reflected in the K constant (10.8), not separately in √3. In three-phase AC circuits, the voltage between line and neutral involves the √3 relationship. The factor 1.732 accounts for the phase angle relationship in three-phase voltage drop calculations. The √3 multiplier is essential for three-phase voltage drop calculations and distinguishes 3-phase from single-phase feeder design.
questions.code_citation: PEC Part 2, Article 2.5.4, Electrical Distribution System Design

questions.explanation: 24 kVAR is only half the required correction and leaves the facility below acceptable PF. 36 kVAR provides insufficient correction; the facility would remain near 0.85 PF. 60 kVAR over-corrects and may swing the power factor into the leading region, creating utility penalties. kVAR = kW × (tan θ₁ − tan θ₂) = 150 × (0.75 − 0.43) = 150 × 0.32 = 48 kVAR. This capacitor bank rating restores the facility to the target 0.92 PF and avoids Meralco penalties. Power factor correction calculations require precise angle (θ) values from PF tables. Over-correction or under-correction both incur utility penalties; the goal is 0.95–0.99 lagging.

questions.text: A 15-story mixed-use building (offices + retail) in Taguig requires a complete electrical distribution system design. Meralco service entrance supplies 13.8 kV primary. Building demand load: 1500 kW (PEC demand factor 0.75). Power factor: 0.92 lagging. Top-floor penthouse load: 180 kW (estimated). Required: Select transformer kVA, calculate service feeder current, specify bus duct system, size the penthouse feeder (200 m run, 380V three-phase), and confirm grounding electrode requirements for clay-loam soil (estimated rho = 50 ohm-m).

options.text: A. 1500 kVA transformer, 2200 A service feeder, dual 1500 A bus ducts, #4/0 AWG penthouse feeder (voltage drop approximately 5.5% over 200 m run), dual ground rods (estimated 2.5 ohm each)
B. 1000 kVA transformer, 1520 A service feeder, single 2000 A bus duct, #4/0 AWG penthouse feeder (acceptable voltage drop 2.8%), single 2.4 m rod (5 ohm)
C. 2000 kVA transformer, 3200 A service feeder, triple 1500 A bus ducts, #500 MCM penthouse feeder (zero voltage drop), dual ground rods with chemical treatment
D. 1500 kVA transformer exceeds calculated demand; use 1000 kVA. Single 2000 A bus duct requires voltage drop monitoring. #2/0 AWG penthouse feeder acceptable if voltage drop <=6% allowed.

questions.rationale: Building demand = 1500 kW x 0.75 = 1125 kW. Apparent power S = 1125 / 0.92 PF = 1222 kVA; select 1500 kVA transformer (next standard size with growth margin). Service feeder current @ 380V three-phase: I = 1222,000 / (sqrt(3) x 380) = 1857 A; select 2200 A feeder. Dual 1500 A bus ducts provide 3000 A capacity (reliability margin). Penthouse feeder: I = 180,000 / (sqrt(3) x 380 x 0.9 PF) = 304 A. Voltage drop for #4/0 AWG (107.2 mm2 copper) over 200 m: Vd = sqrt(3) x rho_cu(75C) x L x I / A = sqrt(3) x 0.0213 x 200 x 304 / 107.2 = 20.9 V = 5.5% of 380V (marginal but acceptable per PEC Article 2.5.4 total voltage drop allowance up to 5% for feeders and 5% for branches; combined design budget). #2/0 AWG (67.4 mm2) would yield Vd = 33.2 V = 8.75% (clearly unacceptable), confirming #4/0 is the minimum compliant conductor. Grounding in clay-loam (rho = 50 ohm-m): single 2.4 m rod ~5-6 ohm (marginal); dual rods spaced 2.4 m apart reduce to ~2.5 ohm (safe). Option a is the correct answer with revised conductor size (#4/0 AWG) and corrected drop percentage (~5.5%). Option b uses an undersized 1000 kVA transformer (insufficient for 1222 kVA demand). Option c over-specifies (2000 kVA exceeds need; 'zero voltage drop' is physically impossible). Option d allows a non-compliant #2/0 AWG.
questions.code_citation: PEC Part 2, Articles 2.5.4, 2.6.1–2.6.3; Part 4, Articles 4.1.3, 4.2.1; Part 5, Articles 5.3.3–5.3.4; Comprehensive Building Distribution Design
